did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter begins with a musical heading: “For the director of music. Do not destroy,” along with the attribution “A miktam of David.”
Did you know? The psalmist addresses the “sons of men” and asks whether they truly speak justly and judge fairly, placing the question of justice at the center of the chapter.
Did you know? The chapter contrasts the heart with the hands: the wicked devise injustices in their hearts, and their actions bring violence upon the earth.

Did you know? Describing the wicked as having “gone astray from the womb” and having “wandered from birth” is a powerful poetic picture of their persistent inclination to lie, not a literal biographical description.
Did you know? The behavior of the wicked is compared to a snake’s venom: their fury is called “the venom of a snake,” emphasizing the danger and harm they cause.
Did you know? The snake in this chapter is portrayed as stopping its ears and refusing to hear the voice of the charmers—in other words, the wicked are shown as refusing attempts to influence them.
Did you know? David uses the image of a lion to describe the threatening power of the wicked and prays, “Break their teeth in their mouths”—break their power to prey.
Did you know? These verses contain a series of images depicting the enemies’ collapse: water flowing away and dispersing, an arrow that fails to strike its target, and a snail melting along its path.
Did you know? The chapter portrays the downfall of the wicked before they can mature and grow strong, using the image of thorn bushes being swept away before the fire can heat them.

Did you know? Near the end of the chapter, the righteous person responds to judgment: he rejoices when he sees justice carried out and washes his feet in the blood of the wicked—a stark poetic expression of the triumph of justice.
Did you know? The final verse summarizes the message with a general conclusion: the righteous will have a reward for their actions, and there is a God who judges on earth.
